text: Nozick's tracking theory adds the sensitivity condition ('if p were false, S would not believe p'). A notorious consequence is that Nozick is led to deny epistemic closure. Why does sensitivity generate closure failure?
choices: Sensitivity is trivially satisfied by every true belief, so it cannot discriminate known entailments from unknown ones.

S can be sensitive to an ordinary p (e.g. 'I have hands') yet fail to be sensitive to an entailed q (e.g. 'I am not a handless brain-in-a-vat'), because in the nearest world where q is false S would still believe q.
Sensitivity requires S to actually deduce every logical consequence of p, and no finite believer can carry out infinitely many deductions.
Sensitivity is equivalent to the safety condition, and safety is well known to be closed under entailment.
explanation: In the nearest world where 'I am a brain-in-a-vat' is true, S would still believe he is not one, so the belief in the entailed skeptical denial is insensitive even though the belief in 'I have hands' is sensitive; hence S can know p without knowing a q that p obviously entails. Nozick embraces this failure of transmission as an anti-skeptical result. Option 3 is doubly wrong: sensitivity is roughly the converse of safety, and it is precisely tracking's failure to transmit across entailment that yields the closure denial.
